about: Psalm 118 in the Vulgate numbering (Psalm 119 in Hebrew) is an acrostic: twenty-two stanzas of eight verses, one stanza for each letter of the Hebrew alphabet, with all eight verses of a stanza beginning with the same letter in the Hebrew. It is the longest psalm in the psalter, and nearly every verse of it speaks about one thing — God's law, which the psalm calls by many names: law, testimony, statute, commandment, judgment, word. This stanza carries the letter HE. In the Roman breviary its verses open the psalmody of Sunday Terce, and the antiphon of that hour in the psalter is drawn from verse 35. The psalm itself runs across all four of Sunday's little hours. Verse thirty-four — “Da mihi intelléctum, et scrutábor legem tuam” — gave this edition its name. In it, the psalmist asks God for understanding and says that he will search His law and keep it with his whole heart.

about_citations.title: United States Conference of Catholic Bishops, Psalm 119

s01.translation: Set before me for a law, O Lord, the way of Thy statutes, and I will seek it always.

s02.translation: Give me understanding, and I will search Thy law, and I will keep it with my whole heart.

s03.translation: Lead me into the path of Thy commandments, for that is the very thing I have wanted.

s04.translation: Incline my heart to Thy testimonies, and not to greed.

s05.translation: Turn away my eyes, that they may not look on emptiness; give me life in Thy way.

s06.translation: Establish Thy word for Thy servant, in Thy fear.

s07.translation: Cut away the reproach I have feared, for Thy judgments are delightful.

s08.translation: Behold, I have longed for Thy commandments; give me life in Thy justice.

w001.function: A predicative accusative with “viam” (w005): the way is to be established as a law.

w002.function: An imperative governing two accusatives: “viam” (w005) and the predicate “Legem” (w001).

w006.function: A genitive plural depending on “viam” (w005). Here “iustificatiónes” means statutes.

w009.function: The form is shared by the future indicative and present subjunctive. This translation reads the future: “I will seek.” The Hebrew expresses a resolve to keep the way, and the Nova Vulgata renders it with the unambiguous future “servabo.”

function_citations.title: Allen and Greenough, New Latin Grammar

w009.note: The ending -am is future indicative and present subjunctive at once. I shall seek it, or that I may seek it, after the imperative pone. This edition takes the future and marks the doubt.

w010.function: The pronoun refers to “viam” (w005). Likewise, the Greek pronoun αὐτήν in the Septuagint refers to ὁδόν, “the way.”

w014.function: The object of the petition “Da” (w012): the psalmist asks God for the gift of understanding.

w015.function: Here the conjunction links the petition to the psalmist's statement of what he will do.

w016.function: After the petition “Da” (w012), the psalmist says that he will search God's law.

w020.function: The verb form is ambiguous like “exquíram” (w009) — future indicative or present subjunctive — but here the coordinate “scrutábor” (w016), unambiguously future, decides: this edition reads the future.

function_citations.title: Allen and Greenough, New Latin Grammar

w024.function: Ablative with “in” (w022). The phrase “in toto corde” stresses that God's law is to be kept with a whole and undivided heart.

w026.function: Imperative — “Deduc” takes the shortened form without final -e, like “dic” and “duc”.

w033.function: An intensive pronoun referring to “sémitam” (w029): that very one.

w044.function: Accusative after “in” (w043): the direction the heart might lean instead.

w048.function: Opens a negative purpose clause, hence the subjunctive at “vídeant” (w049).

w049.function: Subjunctive after “ne” (w048): not a statement but the purpose for which the turning is asked.

w050.function: Here “vánitas” means emptiness or futility, not conceit.

w067.function: Relative pronoun in the accusative, object of “suspicátus” (w068).

w068.function: Perfect participle of a deponent verb. With “sum” (w069) it forms one finite verb.

w069.function: With “suspicátus” (w068), it forms the perfect of a deponent verb: I have feared.

w071.function: A nominative plural with the verb are understood.

w073.function: Predicate to the understood “are”, agreeing with “iudícia” (w071).

w075.function: The object “mandáta” (w076) names what the psalmist longs for: God's commandments.

w079.function: An ablative governed by in: “according to thy justice”.

w081.function: It repeats “vivífica” (w054) from the earlier verse.
